Volume 14 · Chapter 09

Intermediaries, liquidity and leverage cycles

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v14-c08

By the endAnalyze financial-sector amplification and endogenous risk.

Volume14 · Chapter9

Intermediaries, liquidity and leverage cycles

Capability. Reconcile an intermediary’s capital and funding, prove the incentives behind a liquidity-providing deposit contract and a run, solve a price-impact feedback example, and derive how constrained risk-bearing changes asset prices. Five original worked cases and twelve solved exercises expose the assumptions behind each mechanism.

Prerequisites. Financial statements and risk measurement from Volumes7 and11; finite equilibrium and game theory from Volume13; household pricing and constrained investment from Chapters7–8. All policy caps, payoffs and numerical data here are synthetic. No current regulatory ratio or actual bank condition is asserted.

A solvent bank can face a withdrawal demand larger than its immediately available cash. A bank can also have negative economic equity even while receiving a temporary cash loan. An asset can be easy to sell in small quantities while a large forced sale moves its price. These are different questions. Diagnose the balance sheet, timing and feasible trades before treating all three as a lack of liquidity.

1. Capital absorbs losses; liquidity meets dated payments

Write marked asset value A, debt D and equity n=A−D. For n>0, asset leverage is L=A/n. A change ΔA with fixed debt changes equity one-for-one: Δn=ΔA. Its percentage impact is Δn/n=L(ΔA/A). This accounting exposure is not a probability of failure and says nothing by itself about when debt must be paid. A debt maturity schedule, liquid reserves, collateral restrictions and access to funding determine payment feasibility.

A minimum equity fraction h∈(0,1) against a specified asset exposure imposes n≥hA, equivalently A≤n/h. If a position is financed by borrowing against its value with haircut h, its own-funds requirement has the same algebra, although a haircut contract and a capital regulation are different institutions. Scope matters: a cap on risky exposures is not automatically a cap on all accounting assets, and a margin demand can change before any terminal default occurs.

Worked case1: A small asset loss forces a large balance-sheet adjustment

Start with assets100,debt90 and equity10. A five-unit marked asset loss leaves assets95,equity5 and leverage19. Suppose the synthetic cap is assets/equity≤10. At unchanged sale prices, selling45 of assets and repaying45 of debt leaves assets50,debt45,equity5. The required sale is45, even though the original asset loss was only5.

Alternatively, an equity injection of4.5 immediately used to repay debt retains assets95 with debt85.5 and equity9.5, meeting the cap. If the injected cash stays on the balance sheet and also counts as an asset, the required injection instead solves(95+e)/(5+e)=10, giving5. Stating what happens to injected cash prevents an inconsistent capital calculation. These transactions redistribute claims and funding; none reverses the original loss of asset value.

Forced sales can alter the quoted prices used in these calculations, while collateral haircuts can rise at the same time. We first study liquidity insurance and strategic withdrawals, then make price feedback explicit.

2. A deposit contract provides insurance against private timing needs

There are dates0,1,2 and a unit mass of depositors, each endowed with one good at date0. A fixed fraction λ∈(0,1) learns privately at date1 that it must consume then; the remaining fraction can wait until date2. The exact cross-sectional fraction is a model primitive, not an unproved law of large numbers for independently sampled continuum agents. An early type values u(c1); a patient type values u(c1+c2), since date1 goods can be stored at gross return one until date2.

A unit of storage returns one at either later date. A long investment returns R>1 at date2 or one if liquidated at date1. The bank pools the initial goods, stores x and invests1−x long. With verifiable types, an efficient allocation consumes only at the date each type needs, satisfies λc1+(1−λ)c2/R=1, and maximizes λu(c1)+(1−λ)u(c2). Positive interior optimality requires u′(c1)=Ru′(c2). The resource set is compact and utility continuous, so a maximum exists; strict concavity makes the allocation unique.

Use u(c)=−1/(c+κ),κ>0,c≥0. This increasing, strictly concave utility has a finite value at zero, which will matter for the run lottery. It is an original shifted-utility specification, not an assertion that households literally have this preference. The interior condition becomes c2+κ=√R(c1+κ). Combining it with resources gives

c1={1−[(1−λ)/R](√R−1)κ}/{λ+(1−λ)/√R},   c2=√R c1+(√R−1)κ.

The formula requires a positive numerator and feasible positive consumptions; otherwise solve the boundary problem. For the example below both consumptions are positive and c2>c1>1. The bank can implement that no-run allocation by storing x=λc1. A patient depositor then prefers waiting to withdrawing c1 and storing it privately. Private type information therefore does not by itself prevent truthful withdrawals in the good equilibrium.

Worked case2: Solve the insured allocation

Set λ=1/4,R=36/25 and κ=1/10. The unique optimum is c1=95/84, approximately1.13095238, and c2=241/175, approximately1.37714286. Storage is95/336; long investment is241/336. At date2, long output723/700 exactly pays the three-quarters patient mass its promised consumption.

Expected utility is-735/1034, about−0.71083172. An individual who instead invests alone and liquidates when early receives(1,1.44), with expected utility-5/7, about−0.71428571. The pooled allocation is better, even though early consumption rises and patient consumption falls relative to that benchmark: it insures private timing risk. Strict concavity and the proved optimum establish the welfare comparison within this model, without claiming superiority to every possible trading arrangement.

3. The same promise can support a run

Specify the withdrawal game. Depositors put their entire unit into a mutual bank; deposits cannot be sold. At date1 each simultaneously chooses withdrawal or waiting, before learning a random queue position. A withdrawing depositor is paid the fixed c1 while resources last. The bank uses storage and liquidates long assets as necessary. Once exhausted, it pays nothing further. Waiting depositors share any remaining date2 resources. Queue positions are exchangeable so service probabilities equal the served fraction; this service rule is part of the contract.

In the no-run equilibrium, all early types withdraw and patient types wait. Storage covers early payments and patient types obtain c2>c1. An atomistic patient’s deviation does not change aggregates and lowers its consumption; an early type who waits receives no valued date1 consumption. Thus the proposed actions are individually optimal.

Now suppose everybody else withdraws. Total liquidation resources are x+(1−x)=1, below the promised c1>1 per unit mass. A fraction1/c1 is paid and the bank is exhausted. A patient who waits gets zero; a patient who joins the queue gets c1 with probability1/c1 and zero otherwise. Because u(0) is finite and u(c1)>u(0), joining strictly dominates waiting under this belief. Early types also join. All withdrawing is another equilibrium even though the long technology has no risky payoff.

Do not replace the utility in that argument by log c or unshifted −1/c and retain the same strict expected-utility comparison. If the lottery has positive probability of zero, those preferences give expected utility−∞; waiting at zero also gives−∞. The finite-zero assumption or another explicit treatment of subsistence must be supplied. Similarly, when c1≤1 the exhaustion argument changes; dividing by1−f at a withdrawal mass f=1 without checking residual resources is invalid.

Worked case3: Verify the run incentive and a suspension rule

In case2, the all-run service probability is84/95. A patient depositor’s expected queue utility is-970/517, about−1.87620890, strictly above u(0)=−10 from waiting after everyone else exhausts the bank. It is much worse than that patient’s no-run utility; equilibrium behavior need not select the collectively preferred outcome.

Consider a different precommitted contract that stops date1 payments after λ depositors have been paid. It never liquidates the long investment, and any unpaid claimant retains its date2 share. If the actual served mass is w≤λ, total date2 resources for the remaining1−w claimants are R(1−x)+x−wc1. A patient who waits receives

Cwait(w)=[R(1−x)+x−wc1]/(1−w).

Since R(1−x)+x=λc1+(1−λ)c2>c1, this waiting payoff exceeds c1 for every0≤w≤λ. If a patient tries to withdraw and is refused, it keeps the same waiting claim; if served, it receives the smaller c1. Exchangeable queue order gives a positive probability of service to a would-be withdrawer, so waiting strictly dominates withdrawal. Thus patient types wait, early types are served, and the good allocation results.

The proof uses a known fixed early fraction and enforceable suspension. If more people genuinely need date1 consumption, the fixed cutoff can deny them insurance. It also assumes an unpaid claimant retains its date2 right. Confiscating that right on refusal would define a different game.

A credible externally funded date2 guarantee exceeding c1 can likewise make patients prefer waiting. But its off-equilibrium payments require resources and a credible commitment. With risky assets, uncertain liquidity needs or other bank actions, incentive and fiscal costs must be modeled. An announcement that no depositor will lose does not prove that the required goods or funding are available.

The 2015 Diamond–Dybvig teaching slides explain the withdrawal game and explicitly flag the finite-zero-utility issue. The shifted-utility economy, exact allocations and suspension verification above are original; they do not replicate the full1983 article or its variable-liquidity-need extension.

4. Marked losses and forced sales can reinforce one another

Consider a separate static market with aggregate bank holdings K>0 of one asset and fixed initial debt D. Banks are atomistic price takers, but their aggregate sales affect market price. If they sell z at common price p and use all sale proceeds to repay debt, the remaining balance sheet is

assets=p(K−z),   debt=D−pz,   equity=pK−D.

A sale at the marking price leaves equity unchanged conditional on that price. It reduces assets and debt together. Require positive equity, nonnegative remaining debt and0≤z≤K. A synthetic leverage cap L>1 requires p(K−z)≤L(pK−D). A bank retaining as much of the asset as the cap permits therefore supplies z=max{0,LD/p−(L−1)K}, provided this is feasible. The retention preference is a stipulated bank objective; it is not claimed to follow from every shareholder utility.

Outside buyers have sufficient cash and quasilinear value V(z)=p0z−αz²/2, α>0. Maximizing V(z)−pz gives inverse demand p=p0−αz at an interior purchase. Its decreasing price reflects the opportunity cost of placing progressively more assets with outsiders. This is not an estimated empirical demand curve. Competitive consistency requires the price and the banks’ required sales to solve both equations.

For an interior constrained solution, substitute inverse demand:

[z+(L−1)K](p0−αz)=LD.

This quadratic may have two roots, one, or none. Every algebraic root must still satisfy positive price, positive equity, nonnegative debt, the sales interval, the bank’s active-cap branch and the buyer’s feasible budget. An algebraic solution with an insolvent bank is not a functioning positive-equity leverage equilibrium.

One possible adjustment procedure repeatedly recalculates required sales at the preceding quoted price, F(z)=LD/(p0−αz)−(L−1)K. At an interior fixed point its derivative is F′(z)=LDα/p². Local convergence of this particular iteration requires F′<1; with F′>1 small iteration errors grow. This is a statement about a specified update rule. Static equilibrium alone does not imply that real institutions follow it or select its attracting branch.

Worked case4: Two self-consistent deleveraging prices

Take K=1,D=0.805,L=5,p0=1,α=0.2 and ample buyer cash. The cap equation becomes(z+4)(1−0.2z)=4.025, or z²−z+0.125=0. Its two roots are(0.1464466094, 0.8535533906), exactly(1∓√(1/2))/2. Prices are(0.9707106781, 0.8292893219), and equity values are(0.1657106781, 0.0242893219).

Remaining debt is(0.6628427125, 0.0971572875); remaining asset value is five times equity at both roots. All quantities are positive and sales are below the original unit, so both roots pass the economic feasibility checks. The update derivatives are(0.8543115272, 1.1705331933). The low-sale branch is locally attracting under the stated iteration and the high-sale branch is repelling. The claim is not a general selection theorem.

Raise D to0.82 while keeping all other primitives. On0≤z≤1 the left-hand side4+0.2z−0.2z² is at most4.05, whereas LD=4.1. No feasible active-cap solution exists, and zero sales violates the cap. The largest debt admitting a root is0.81, at z=0.5. A missing compliant equilibrium means the specified rules need another mechanism—new equity, creditor losses, a changed cap or resolution—not that assets can be sold for a negative price to make the arithmetic work.

The opening of Brunnermeier and Pedersen’s advance-access paper distinguishes market liquidity from funding liquidity and motivates their feedback through capital and margins. Our exact quadratic bank example is a different original model; it does not reproduce their margin-setting theory or quantitative findings.

5. Risk-bearing capacity changes the clearing price

To isolate risk-bearing, use a separate one-period financial-wealth model. A claim pays Y∼N(μ,σ²),μ>0,σ²>0, with positive net supply X. Dealer j has utility−exp(−ajW′),aj>0, over signed terminal financial wealth. Buying xj claims at price p gives W′=Wj+(Y−p)xj, with the safe gross return normalized to one. A mandate limits purchases to0≤pxj≤Cj,Cj>0. Dealers have cash at least Cj; the cap is not a borrowing assumption.

Normal Y can be negative, and terminal wealth can be negative; exponential utility is defined on all real wealth. This exact CARA-normal calculation is therefore a stylized financial-wealth problem, not a positive-consumption or limited-liability bank model. The financial claim includes its signed settlement obligation. The outside seller supplies X and receives the buyers’ price payments; purchases and sale proceeds are transfers, while the payoff distribution is a primitive.

The normal moment-generating formula gives expected utility−exp[−ajWj−aj(μ−p)x+(aj²σ²/2)x²]. Maximizing it is exactly equivalent to maximizing(μ−p)x−ajσ²x²/2. This strict concavity gives the unique demand

xj(p)=min{max[(μ−p)/(ajσ²),0],Cj/p},   p>0.

For0<p<μ each uncapped and capped branch is continuous and strictly decreasing, so their minimum and the sum of demands are continuous and strictly decreasing. As p approaches zero from above, each positive cash cap Cj/p diverges and demand approaches μ/(ajσ²). As p approaches μ, all demands approach zero. Therefore if0<X<Σμ/(ajσ²), the intermediate-value theorem gives a unique price in(0,μ) that clears the market. At equality the candidate limiting price is zero and lies outside the stipulated positive-price model; do not silently include it.

Without active caps, aggregate demand yields p=μ−σ²X/(Σ1/aj). With caps, solve the relevant piecewise equation and verify each dealer’s branch. Exogenous wealth W by itself does not change unconstrained CARA demand; changing a capacity C is the mechanism here. Quietly replacing a fixed risk-aversion coefficient with the inverse of wealth would define different preferences.

Worked case5: One dealer’s reduced mandate lowers the price

Set μ=1.2,σ²=0.04,X=2 and a1=a2=2. With C1=1.5,C2=3, the unique price is1.12, each dealer buys one, and neither cap binds. The expected excess gross return is μ/p−1=1/14.

Reduce only C1 to0.54. At the new price1.08, dealer1 holds0.54/1.08=0.5 and dealer2 holds(1.2−1.08)/0.08=1.5. Dealer1 would like1.5 absent its cap, confirming that it binds; dealer2 spends1.62, below its cap3. Supply2 clears. The expected excess return is now1/9. Fundamentals μ and σ² have not changed; the marginal holder’s allocation and required compensation have.

The model has one risky claim and a normal payoff. It does not say that all observed spread changes reveal intermediary constraints, or that a guarantee increases welfare. Identifying such a mechanism in data requires an exogenous capacity change, correctly measured payoffs and evidence about the institutions that actually absorb the risk.

6. A mechanism-based crisis diagnosis

Begin with dated cash flows and a marked balance sheet. Separate an inability to meet near-term withdrawals from a negative net asset value, while recognizing that forced liquidation can connect them. Identify whose constraint binds: a depositor’s timing need, a dealer’s cash mandate, a lender’s collateral rule or a bank’s leverage cap. Record what prices move and what transactions repay debt rather than create new goods.

Distinguish fundamental news from endogenous amplification. Falling asset prices may reveal lower expected payoffs, respond to forced sales, or reflect a change in the risk-bearing sector. A model fitting the price fall alone does not identify the channel. Useful additional observations include withdrawal timing, funding terms, security-level sales, ownership changes and counterpart balance sheets; each requires its own measurement and identification argument.

A backstop can change equilibrium incentives while generating contingent fiscal exposure. Recapitalization changes who owns residual risk; liquidity lending adds a dated claim that must be repaid or absorbed; suspension changes access to consumption. Evaluate those transactions within a stated resource and incentive model. This chapter supplies exact mechanisms and boundary cases, not a universal policy ranking.

7. Exercises

  1. Change the marked asset loss in case1 from5 to7. Compute equity, leverage and the sale needed to restore the cap10 at unchanged sale prices. Reconcile remaining assets and debt. Explain why the calculation fails if equity is nonpositive.
  2. Derive the shifted-utility insured allocation, including the positivity requirement. In case2 change the early fraction to1/2. Compute both consumption promises and initial storage, and verify incentive compatibility and the resource equation.
  3. Prove both withdrawal equilibria for the original case2 contract. State why random queue order, atomistic behavior, finite u(0), c1>1 and patient access to storage matter. Which part fails if u(c)=log c is substituted without changing the zero-payoff lottery?
  4. Independently compute the original all-run service probability and expected utility. Compare with the patient’s no-run utility and with waiting after everyone else runs. Distinguish an individual deviation comparison from an ex ante welfare comparison.
  5. Prove the suspension-rule waiting inequality for every served mass0≤w≤λ. Explain what happens if the actual early mass is0.4 while the announced cutoff remains0.25, and why the result does not establish optimal insurance under uncertain liquidity demand.
  6. Suppose an external guarantor can credibly supply up to G units of date2 goods in every history, where G=c1+0.05 for the original case2. It tops up every waiting depositor’s date2 payment to at least G. Prove why patient types wait and why the total transfer never exceeds the available G for a unit mass of depositors. Does zero realized payment in the good equilibrium prove the promise has no opportunity or incentive cost outside this model?
  7. Derive the fire-sale quadratic and all balance-sheet feasibility conditions. For the original K,D,L,p0 but α=0.1, solve the roots, retain the feasible solution and calculate its price. Explain why discarding an out-of-range root is an economic-domain check, not evidence of universal equilibrium uniqueness.
  8. With α=0.2 derive the maximum debt permitting a compliant positive-equity root. Show the two-root, repeated-root and no-root cases. Calculate the update derivative at the repeated root and explain the limits of calling a branch stable.
  9. Derive CARA-normal demand from expected utility and prove existence/uniqueness of the positive clearing price under the stated supply bound. In case5 reduce C1 further to0.265, keeping C2=3. Solve price and both holdings, check caps, and calculate the expected excess return.
  10. For the original case5 parameters, derive the smallest C1 that leaves the uncapped price unchanged when C2=3. Explain why reducing initial wealth W1 without changing its feasible cap need not change CARA demand, and state the consistency requirement between cash and the mandate.
  11. A dealer starts with asset exposure100,debt90,equity10 and an equity requirement h=0.1. A marked loss of5 coincides with a rise of h to0.2. At unchanged sale prices, find its maximum allowed exposure, required sale and remaining debt. Compare with the fixed-h calculation and state why it does not by itself estimate a causal liquidity spiral.
  12. A crisis memo calls every loss a liquidity shortage, treats all lower prices as fundamental news, and proposes an uncosted guarantee. Write a corrected decision protocol with balance-sheet and timing tests, a competing price mechanism, counterpart accounts, a credible guarantee constraint and a falsifiable empirical prediction. Give explicit grading criteria.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. A larger marked loss

Assets become93 and debt remains90, so equity is3 and leverage31. The cap allows assets30; selling63 and repaying the same amount leaves debt27, assets30 and equity3. Positive equity is needed for the leverage ratio and for the cap to permit a positive asset book. With n≤0, rearranging A≤10n cannot authorize a negative asset exposure as a normal operating solution; recapitalization, creditor loss allocation or resolution must be specified.

2. More early consumers

u′(c)=1/(c+κ)², so the positive interior first-order condition gives c2+κ=√R(c1+κ). Substitution into resources yields the formula in Section2, requiring positive c1 and feasible nonnegative c2. Strict concavity proves global optimality for the positive interior candidate. With λ=1/2 the solution is(13/12,33/25) and storage13/24. Long investment11/24 yields0.66 at date2, paying half the population1.32. Patient consumption1.32 exceeds the withdrawal1.083333…, so patient types prefer waiting. Both promises exceed zero and the resource equality holds exactly.

3. Two individual best-response systems

With only the early mass withdrawing, storage pays λc1 and the long investment pays the waiting patient mass c2>c1. An atomistic patient cannot change that aggregate outcome and would lose by withdrawing. An early type needs date1 consumption and withdraws. When everyone else runs, total resources1 are exhausted because c1>1. Waiting pays zero; a random queue position gives positive service probability1/c1, so finite u(0) and increasing utility make joining strictly better. Exchangeability determines the probability and the atomistic convention makes a unilateral action unable to save an exhausted bank. Patient storage makes early receipt c1 available for later consumption, so waiting must beat that value. With log utility, the queue lottery has expected utility−∞ and waiting at zero also has−∞. The displayed strict expected-utility inequality is then unavailable; one must revise the domain or payoff specification rather than claim the original proof still works.

4. Correct comparison of run payoffs

Probability of service is84/95. Since c1+0.1=517/420, utility when served is−420/517 and utility when unserved is−10. Their probability-weighted mean is−970/517≈−1.87620890. The patient’s no-run utility is−1/(241/175+1/10)=-350/517, approximately−0.67698259, which is better. But a unilateral waiter facing everyone else’s run obtains−10, which is worse than joining. The best-response comparison holds others’ actions fixed; the welfare comparison changes their actions and the aggregate liquidation. Confusing those comparisons would erase the coordination problem.

5. What suspension proves

Subtract c1 from Cwait(w). The difference is[R(1−x)+x−c1]/(1−w)=(1−λ)(c2−c1)/(1−w)>0 for0≤w≤λ<1. A served patient withdrawer receives less; an unserved one retains the same claim, so the positive service chance makes trying to withdraw strictly inferior. With actual early mass0.4 and a0.25 cutoff, at least0.15 of the population with genuine early needs cannot be served even if all patient types wait. Their date2 claims do not replace desired date1 consumption. A rule eliminating a particular run can therefore fail to insure an unforeseen aggregate liquidity need; the fixed-fraction proof is not an optimal-contract theorem for random demand.

6. A funded guarantee

A patient who waits receives at least G>c1, exceeding even a successful early withdrawal stored until date2. Thus waiting strictly dominates joining the queue; early types still value date1 payment. At most one unit mass can wait. Each top-up is max{G−bank payment,0}≤G, so aggregate transfers are at most G and the stated external capacity funds every history. Here G=248/210, about1.18095238, below the good-equilibrium c2, so no top-up is actually made in that equilibrium. This does not show that committing resources, financing them or changing bank risk incentives is free in a richer model. The proof assumes the capacity and enforceability that an empirical policy evaluation must substantiate.

7. A shallower outside demand curve

After sales, equity is pK−D and the active leverage cap gives p(K−z)=L(pK−D), hence z=LD/p−(L−1)K. Combining with p=p0−αz yields the quadratic. Require0≤z≤K,p>0,pK>D,D−pz≥0 and the correct positive-sale branch, along with buyer affordability. At α=0.1 it becomes z²−6z+0.25=0, with roots(6∓√35)/2. Only the smaller root0.0419601085 lies in[0,1]. Its price is0.9958039892; equity and remaining debt are positive and the cap binds. The other root exceeds the entire initial holding. This establishes one feasible root for these primitives, not uniqueness under every slope or balance sheet.

8. A boundary of feasible deleveraging

For the fixed K=1,L=5,p0=1,α=0.2, the left side is4+0.2z−0.2z², maximized at z=1/2 with value4.05. Thus the maximum debt compatible with an active-cap root is4.05/5=0.81. At D=0.805 both previously computed roots are feasible; at0.81 the repeated root has p=0.9,equity0.09,remaining assets0.45 and debt0.36; at0.82 no root exists. Its update derivative is LDα/p²=5(0.81)(0.2)/0.9²=1. Linear contraction does not hold at that boundary. A slope below one proves local convergence of the stated smooth iteration, not an equilibrium-selection or welfare theorem about unspecified market dynamics.

9. Less constrained risk-bearing

Apply the normal MGF to the exponential of−a(Y−p)x. Taking its exponent and preserving the sign of the negative exponential gives the equivalent objective(μ−p)x−aσ²x²/2, a strictly concave quadratic. Its unconstrained optimum is(μ−p)/(aσ²); clip to[0,C/p]. On(0,μ), both component branches decrease strictly and continuously, so aggregate demand does too. Its limits at the endpoints bracket X under the stated strict supply bound, giving existence and uniqueness. With C1=0.265 the price is1.06; holdings are(0.25,1.75). Dealer1 spends0.265 and would prefer1.75 without its cap; dealer2 spends1.855<3 and is interior. They hold total2. Expected excess return is(1.2−1.06)/1.06=7/53. All conclusions concern the signed-wealth, normal-payoff model actually solved.

10. Capacity versus CARA wealth

The uncapped price is1.12 with each dealer holding one. Therefore C1 must be at least1.12 to preserve that allocation; dealer2’s cap3 is already slack. At equality the constraint can bind with zero multiplier. Initial wealth W multiplies expected exponential utility by a positive constant exp(−aW) and does not change its unconstrained maximizer. A wealth reduction affects demand here only if it changes feasibility or another primitive. The stated cash-financed mandate requires available cash at least C; lowering wealth below the mandate without changing that funding assumption would make the proposed feasible set inconsistent. Wealth-dependent relative-risk-aversion preferences would be a different model.

11. Losses and a tighter requirement

After the loss, assets95 and equity5 face h=0.2, allowing maximum exposure25. The dealer sells70 and repays70, leaving debt20 and equity5. With unchanged h=0.1 it would sell45 and hold50; the stricter requirement adds25 to sales at fixed prices. An observed correlation among prices, haircuts and sales could also reflect common fundamental news or lender anticipation. A causal liquidity-spiral claim needs a model or identification strategy for how sales change prices and how those prices change constraints; these balance-sheet identities alone do not estimate either response.

12. A ten-point decision protocol

Condition and timing,2points: report marked assets, liabilities, equity and near-term payment demands, distinguishing missing cash from insolvency. Competing price mechanisms,2points: compare payoff news with constrained-holder sales or changing risk-bearing; specify data that would discriminate them. Counterparts,2points: reconcile sale proceeds, creditor repayment, new lending and any government claims without adding transfers to output. Credibility and resources,2points: state the guarantor’s worst-case funding capacity and timing, recipient eligibility and incentives; do not infer credible capacity from a promise. Falsification,2points: predeclare an observable prediction such as concentrated sales by institutions facing an independently identified cap change and absorption by less-constrained buyers; explain what absence, reversal or fundamental-news evidence would weaken the mechanism. Equivalent rigorous protocols earn credit; a blanket guarantee without a resource account or a label applied to every crisis does not.

8. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain why deposit insurance, an equity injection and an asset purchase are different interventions. A sound explanation identifies the withdrawal incentive and guarantor’s contingent liability, the change in residual ownership and loss absorption, and the transfer of asset risk and funding between seller and buyer. Do not claim that any of them mechanically restores lost real output.

One-week check. (1) What happens to equity after an asset sale at its marking price with proceeds repaying debt? (2) Which utility boundary makes the strict random-queue run argument valid? (3) Does a quadratic root prove a feasible deleveraging equilibrium? (4) What changes pricing in case5 when payoff moments remain fixed? Answers: equity stays pK−D conditional on p; u(0) must be finite for the stated strict comparison; no, solvency, debt, holdings, branch and buyer budgets must also hold; the binding dealer capacity changes who bears the risk. Redo Exercises1,3,7 or9 after an error and transfer the corrected reasoning to new parameters.
